awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Machine-Learning Enabled Analog-to-Digital Converter
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial impacts of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project are in developing electronic components called analog to digital converters (ADCs). Physical phenomena like light waves exist in analog domain, whereas chip circuits require digital values. ADCs turn real world analog measurements into digital values that are used in computers. This project enhances scientific and technological understanding of the ADC process by demonstrating a new approach based on machine learning (ML). Computer models suggest that this new, patent-pending approach can measure much denser signals than traditional ADCs, meaning more information can be captured and processed. The first market opportunity will be computer chips that send data over networks, enabling faster data center and internet connections. The devices using this technology will have significant higher speeds and have cost advantages over traditional devices. The existing data center ADC market is close to $1 billion annually and growing. 

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project advances the design of ADCs. The ML ADC decomposes an analog signal into multiple channels, each containing only a portion of the signal’s total information. Each channel is sampled separately, slower than the input signal’s Nyquist rate, producing aliased and complicated digital outputs. A neural network, trained to approximate the inverse transfer function of the analog front-end, maps those digital outputs to the standard Shannon-Nyquist signal representation. This project implements one half of a common communication device, a Serializer/Deserializer receiver, using a ML ADC in printed circuit board prototype form. This project will examine the ability of the physical prototype to capture complete information in gigahertz-range pulse amplitude modulated (PAM) signals. This project expects to replicate computer simulations indicating high accuracy of the ML ADC when driven by a jittery and phase-drifting clock running below the Nyquist rate. The project will produce neural network models trained on the receiver’s data and report the error rates achieved by the models in decoding PAM-4 signals recorded by the receiver.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
A New Paradigm for Signal Processing

The core achievement of this Phase I project, funded by the American taxpayers, was the successful design and validation of a revolutionary "machine-learning enabled" analog-to-digital converter (ADC). Historically, converting real-world analog signals (like radio waves or light pulses) into digital data required hyper-precise circuits that were extremely sensitive to timing errors, such as jitter.

We have fundamentally disrupted this approach by shifting the complexity from analog circuitry to machine-learning. Instead of trying to build a perfect circuit, we developed a system that breaks an incoming signal into a set of frequency features using simplified analog components. We then used a neural network to reconstruct the original signal. Neural networks are very good at dealing with messy information, and our experiments showed that our network can accommodate imperfect timing information. Our findings proved that this system could maintain perfect accuracy even when subjected to extreme timing distortions that would cause traditional hardware to fail.

The significance of this project is that it solves a critical bottleneck in the global digital infrastructure. As the world moves toward 400 GB/s data speeds to support Generative AI and hyperscale datacenters, traditional copper cables are hitting physical speed limits. Our jitter-resilient SerDes is the key to unlocking higher speeds by enabling denser data-encoding protocols that were previously too fragile to deploy.

  • Our technology allows companies to upcycle existing copper and fiber lines, increasing their data capacity without the environmental and financial cost of deploying new fiber lines or replacing massive amounts of copper cabling.

  • By unlocking a solution to the 400 GB/s bottleneck, we ensure that American innovation and computing power remains at the forefront of the global high speed computing market.

Summary of Outcomes Over the course of this award, we progressed from numerical simulations to a fully functional hardware-in-the-loop prototype. We successfully demonstrated that we could achieve industry standard bit error rates under radical clock drift and jitter.  As context, we can tolerate roughly one million times more timing jitter than traditional SerDes.

In our Phase I project, we successfully demonstrated:

  1. System Integration: Assembled a mock communication link using off-the-shelf components and our custom filter array to prove hardware viability.

  2. Baseline Feasibility: Verified the fundamental logic of our system by achieving a perfect record over 1 billion test examples under ideal timing. 

  3. Resilience Stress Tests: Maintained industry-standard performance under radical 1% clock drift and 100% clock cycle jitter—conditions that far exceed the limits of traditional converters.

  4. Drop-In Compatibility: Proved our system works with standard error-correction codes (Reed-Solomon), ensuring it can be integrated into current networking products without requiring a total redesign of industry standards.

This project has successfully provided the technical proof of concept and commercial market discovery necessary to move toward a full-scale silicon microchip in Phase II.
